slides.title: One task, one analysis tool
slides.notes: This table is the spine of the hour. Each row gets two or three slides.

rows.text: Do the outputs track the targets across the whole range?
Which classes are confused, and at what threshold?
Distance matrix, hit histogram, weight planes
How many groups are there, and what defines each?
Is there any pattern left in the errors?

runs.text: Always run the analysis on the training, validation and test sets separately.

slides.title: Fitting: the regression plot
slides.notes: The outlier here might be a phone with a faulty battery, or a wrong record. The plot does not say which; it says where to look.

ops.xTitle: Target t: real minutes of battery left

runs.text: Plot every output against its target
A perfect network puts every point on the line a = t.
Fit a straight line a = m t + c through the points. Good: m near 1, c near 0.
R, the correlation coefficient, measures how tightly the points hug that line. R near 1 is good.
One point sits far below the line: an outlier worth checking by hand.

slides.title: Reading R, and what it hides
slides.notes: Also useful: a histogram of the errors. It should be centred on zero and roughly bell-shaped.

runs.text: Reading R, and what it hides
The outputs explain almost all the variation in the targets. R² is the fraction explained: R = 0.95 means about 90%.
A high R is not proof
A few extreme points can lift R while the middle of the range is poor. Always look at the scatter, not only the number.
R = 0.99 on training and 0.80 on test is overfitting. Similar values on all three sets is what you want.
Outliers on the plot are either bad data to remove or rare cases the network needs more examples of.

slides.title: Pattern recognition: the confusion matrix
slides.notes: This is the same payment data as L38, now with a useful model. Note how accuracy went down while usefulness went up.

runs.text: Sensitivity (true positive rate): 85 / 100 = 85% of frauds caught.
Precision: 85 / (85 + 297) = 22% of alarms are real fraud.
Accuracy is 96.9%, lower than the useless "never fraud" model at 99%.

slides.title: The ROC curve: every threshold at once
slides.notes: The area under the curve summarises it in one number: 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is guessing. The curve does not change when classes are imbalanced, which is why it is preferred to accuracy.

runs.text: The ROC curve: every threshold at once
Slide the threshold and trace the trade
The network gives a score from 0 to 1. The threshold turns it into a decision.
Lower the threshold: more frauds caught, more false alarms.
A curve hugging the top-left corner is a good classifier. The diagonal is a coin toss.
The business picks the point: what does a missed fraud cost against an annoyed customer?

slides.title: Clustering: the SOM distance matrix
slides.notes: Also called the U-matrix. It is how you count clusters when you were never told how many there are.

runs.text: Each cell is one neuron. Dark: its weights are far from its neighbours.
Dark ridges are the borders between clusters
After training, measure the distance between the weight vectors of neighbouring neurons.
Light regions: neighbours are alike. This is the inside of one cluster.
A dark band: weights change sharply across it. Two different groups meet here.
Here one ridge splits the map into two groups of customers.

slides.title: Hit histogram and weight planes
slides.notes: Many dead neurons (zero hits) suggest the map is too large for the data. Two summary numbers also exist: quantisation error and topographic error.

runs.text: Hits: how many examples each neuron wins
Weight planes: one map per input
Two more views of the same trained map
Hit histogram: neurons with many hits sit inside clusters. Neurons with zero hits lie on the borders.
Weight plane: the value of one input weight across the grid.
Two planes that look alike mean those inputs are correlated: recharge amount and data used rise together.
A plane that looks different is carrying separate information.

slides.title: Prediction: is anything left in the errors?
slides.notes: White noise errors is the goal. If today's error predicts tomorrow's, the model could have used that and did not.

runs.text: Prediction: is anything left in the errors?
If the network has learnt everything predictable, its errors are random: knowing one tells you nothing about the next.
Then the autocorrelation is a single spike at lag 0 and near zero elsewhere.
Bars standing above the confidence band mean a pattern remains.
The cure is usually longer tapped delay lines, so the network sees further back.

slides.title: The two correlation tests, with their bounds
slides.notes: The cross-correlation bounds are plus or minus 2 times the square root of the product of the error and input autocorrelations at lag 0, divided by root Q. Both tests appear in the Hagan prediction case study, L42.

runs.text: The two correlation tests, with their bounds
e: prediction error. p: input sequence. Q: number of time steps. Values inside the bounds count as zero.
Errors should be unrelated to anything known
Error autocorrelation (first line): errors must not predict later errors. Only τ = 0 may exceed the bounds.
Input-error cross-correlation (third line): the input must not predict the errors, at any lag.
If it does, part of the input effect has not been captured.
The bounds are 95% confidence limits. With Q = 500 they are about ± 9% of the value at lag 0.

slides.title: Check your understanding
slides.notes: Variants ask for fitting (regression plot, R) and clustering (distance matrix, hits, weight planes). The same four-row table answers all of them.

runs.text: Explain the post-training analysis methods used for (a) pattern recognition and (b) prediction networks.
Confusion matrix: sketch the 2 × 2 table; define sensitivity and specificity.
ROC curve: true positive rate against false positive rate as the threshold moves.
Error autocorrelation: formula; should be zero except at lag 0; confidence bounds.
Input-error cross-correlation: should be zero at all lags.
What to do when a test fails: more data, longer delay lines, more neurons.
